intro.html: Writers judge conduct with these words. On the honorable side: ethical and virtuous people do right; probity and rectitude name their honesty and uprightness; propriety and decorum name good, fitting behavior. On the dishonorable side: corrupt and venal people can be bought, nefarious deeds are wicked, and reprehensible ones deserve blame.
Two pairs to sort: probity and rectitude are about honesty and goodness; propriety and decorum are about proper manners. Someone can have perfect decorum and still be corrupt.

words.def: following principles of right conduct; morally right
words.ex: An {ethical} reporter checks every fact before publishing a story.
words.ctx: The company could have hidden the defect and saved millions, but its {ethical} founder insisted on recalling every toy and refunding every family.
words.etym: From Greek ethikos, from ethos, “character, custom.”

mn.cue: EDITH-ICAL: Edith does the right thing
mn.text: When a customer pays twenty dollars too much, Edith runs down the street to give it back. Edith is {ethical}.

scene.alt: A shopkeeper named Edith runs after a customer to return money he overpaid.

words.ex: The {virtuous} shopkeeper returned the lost wallet with every dollar still inside.
words.ctx: The knight was {virtuous} in every way that mattered: he kept his promises, shared his food with strangers and never took credit for another’s deed.

mn.text: Sir Omar keeps every promise, shares his bread and never tells a lie: he is very true and very good. He is {virtuous}.

labels.text: VERY TRUE-ous: good to the core

scene.alt: A knight in armor gives bread to a grateful grandmother.

words.ex: Out of {propriety}, the guests waited for the host to sit before they began eating.
words.ctx: Grandmother valued {propriety} above all: thank-you notes within a week, no hats at the table and never a raised voice in company.
words.etym: From Latin proprietas, “ownership, fitness,” from proprius (one’s own); the sense “proper behavior” came later.
words.note: Propriety (proper behavior) is not proprietary (owned by someone, as a recipe a company keeps secret).

mn.text: At the fancy dinner, Ivy keeps her napkin on her lap, her elbows off the table and her “thank you” ready. She shows perfect {propriety}.

scene.alt: At a dinner table, a polite girl says thank you while a boy beside her eats messily.

words.def: polite, dignified behavior that suits the occasion
words.ex: The guests at the royal dinner behaved with perfect {decorum}.
words.ctx: The debate began with {decorum}, each speaker waiting politely for a turn, but by the end the two sides were shouting over each other.
words.etym: From Latin decorum, “that which is fitting,” from decor (beauty, grace), the same source as decorate.

mn.cue: DECOR-um: manners to match the fancy DECOR
mn.text: In the grand palace hall, guests bow, speak softly and wait their turn, matching the elegant decor. They show perfect {decorum}.

scene.alt: Two well-dressed guests bow politely before a king in his throne room.

words.ex: The judge was known for her {probity}; no one ever doubted her rulings.
words.ctx: The town chose Mr. Ali to count the money from the fundraiser because of his {probity}: in forty years as the bank’s treasurer, he had never been off by a single penny.
words.etym: From Latin probitas, “uprightness, honesty,” from probus (good, honest), the same root as prove.

mn.cue: PROBE-ITY: probe all you want, it’s honest
mn.text: The inspectors probe every page of Treasurer Lin’s books and find every penny in its place. Her {probity} is complete.

scene.alt: An inspector with a magnifying glass finds a treasurer’s account book perfectly honest.

words.def: moral uprightness; strict honesty and goodness
words.ex: Her {rectitude} made her the obvious choice to guard the prize money.
words.ctx: Even his rivals admired the old captain’s {rectitude}; in fifty years at sea he had never broken a promise, hidden a gift or bent a rule for a friend.
words.etym: From Late Latin rectitudo, “straightness,” from rectus (straight, right), the same root as rectangle.

mn.text: Judge Ada stands as straight as a ruler and lives the same way: she has never told a lie or taken a bribe. Her {rectitude} is famous.

scene.alt: A judge stands straight as a ruler beside the scales of justice.

words.def: dishonest, especially in exchange for money or power
words.ex: The {corrupt} referee was paid to call every play for one team.
words.ctx: For years the {corrupt} inspector approved unsafe buildings in exchange for envelopes of cash, until a reporter followed the money.
words.etym: From Latin corruptus, “spoiled, destroyed,” from corrumpere: com (thoroughly) + rumpere (to break).

mn.text: The referee pockets a bag of coins and calls every play for the team that paid him. Rotten to the core, he is {corrupt}.

scene.alt: A sneaky man slips a bag of money to a referee holding a whistle.

words.def: willing to be bribed; open to doing wrong for money
words.ex: The {venal} guard let anyone through the gate for a gold coin.
words.ctx: The old courts were notoriously {venal}: a rich man could buy any verdict he liked, while a poor one could not even get a hearing.
words.etym: From Latin venalis, “for sale,” from venum (sale), the same root as vend.
words.note: Venal (open to bribes) is not venial (minor and easily forgiven, as a venial fault).

mn.cue: VEND-AL: pay him like a VENDING machine
mn.text: Drop a coin in his hand and the guard opens the gate for anyone, like a vending machine. He is {venal}.

scene.alt: A guard holds out his hand for a coin before letting a sneaky man through the castle gate.

words.ex: The villain’s {nefarious} plan was to steal the town’s clock so everyone would miss the fair.
words.ctx: At first the stranger seemed charming, but his purpose was {nefarious}: he had come to swindle the widow out of her farm.
words.etym: From Latin nefarius, from nefas, “a wrong, a crime”: ne (not) + fas (what is right).

mn.text: Late at night the villain sneaks off with the town clock so that everyone will miss the fair. His scheme is {nefarious}.

scene.alt: A masked villain sneaks through the village at night, carrying off the town clock.

words.ex: Rex behaved {reprehensibly} when he knocked down a little kid’s block tower on purpose.
words.ctx: The coach called the players’ behavior {reprehensible}: they had mocked the losing team, thrown trash on the field and refused to shake hands.
words.etym: From Late Latin reprehensibilis, from reprehendere, “to hold back, rebuke.”

mn.text: Rex knocks over little Theo’s block tower on purpose, and Tia scolds him sharply. Such behavior is {reprehensible}.

scene.alt: A teen knocks over a toddler’s block tower as a woman scolds him.

after.cap: Words of praise and blame for conduct.

after.html: Look-alikes: venal (bribable) and venial (easily forgiven); propriety (proper behavior) and proprietary (owned, private).

items.why: Venal means open to bribery (from Latin venum, “sale”). A small, forgivable fault is venial.

choices: Out of propriety, he removed his hat when he entered the dining hall.
The recipe is a propriety secret of the company.
She has full propriety of the land.
The software is propriety and cannot be copied.
items.why: Propriety means proper behavior. The other sentences need proprietary (owned, private) or property.

items.q: Which word is about good manners rather than honesty?
items.why: Decorum is dignified, fitting behavior. Probity and rectitude are about honesty and moral uprightness.

items.q: True or false: a nefarious plan is a kind and helpful one.
items.why: False. Nefarious means wicked or criminal (Latin ne, not + fas, what is right).
